title: Lesson 1.4 Knowledge Check
description: Five questions on ethics and attribution in AI music. Unlimited attempts; your best score counts.

questions.text: Which four questions does this lesson say every AI music project raises? Select all that apply.
questions.feedback: Consent, likeness, ownership, and disclosure are the four. File format is a technical matter, not an ethical one.

questions.text: According to the United States Copyright Office, a work generated entirely by AI with no human creative contribution is eligible for copyright protection.
questions.feedback: The Copyright Office has said such works are not protectable, while human contributions (lyrics, arrangement choices, edits) can be protected to the extent of that contribution.

questions.text: Which prompt follows the course rule on voice and likeness?
options: Sing this in the voice of [a named famous singer]
Make it sound exactly like [a named band]'s 2015 album
Clone my favorite artist's vocal tone
questions.feedback: Prompt for a type of voice, never a specific real person.

questions.text: A text model summarizes a court case with confident detail. What should you do before repeating any of it?
options: Repeat it; models are trained on legal texts
Verify each claim against a primary source and mark what you cannot confirm
Ask the same model again to be sure
Only repeat the parts that sound plausible
questions.feedback: Models blend jurisdictions, go out of date, and sometimes invent cases. Verification against primary sources is the AI feedback evaluation competency.

questions.text: What must an attribution statement for an AI-assisted song include?
options: The human contributions, the tool and version, and the fact that AI-generated material is included
questions.feedback: Attribution names both human and machine contributions and discloses AI involvement.
